title: When the climb stops ending: cell death, senescence, and cancer

objectives.statement: Calculate, from a crypt's cell count and its renewal interval, how many cells one crypt must lose per day, state the condition that keeps its cell number steady, and use that rate relation to show how small a sustained mismatch between production and loss has to be in order to change the tissue.

Distinguish apoptosis from accidental cell death by what happens to the dying cell's contents and to the tissue around it, explain why that difference matters to an epithelium one cell thick, and explain why a necrotic appearance does not by itself establish whether a dedicated pathway was running.

Explain attachment to the basement membrane as a survival condition for an epithelial cell, predict the consequence for a tissue of a cell that survives detachment, and separate what the evidence on shedding and extrusion establishes from what it leaves unsettled, including the order of death and detachment.

Distinguish cellular senescence from apoptosis and from elapsed time, and state both consequences that follow from a cell which stops dividing permanently and stays in the tissue, without resolving the tension between them.

Explain, using evidence that normal functioning tissue carries driver mutations under positive selection, why a driver mutation is not sufficient for cancer; state what that evidence does and does not settle about whether one is necessary; and name what the surrounding tissue contributes to the outcome.

Given a described tissue, identify which controls of the renewal loop appear to be operating, which appear to have failed and which are untested, name every part of the loop where the imbalance could still sit without narrowing it further than the description allows, and state what the description does not license a reader to conclude.

scenes.title: Where a hundred and seventy-five cells a day go
scenes.contentHtml:
Where a hundred and seventy-five cells a day go

Hold one crypt in mind. About 700 cells, sunk into the wall of your descending colon, its opening facing the lumen. It has been there for years and it still holds about 700 cells.

It has also replaced all of them, roughly every four days, for as long as you have had it.

Lesson 01 of this block (PREM-05.01) did that arithmetic and then left it standing. Seven hundred cells over four days is about 175 new cells a day from one crypt, as a steady-state estimate, and not a statement that every crypt cell lives exactly four days. And it drew the consequence that this lesson exists to explain: for the population to stay constant, cells must leave at the same average rate they are made.

So about 175 cells a day leave one crypt. Not fewer, on average, or cells would accumulate and the crypt would grow. Not more, or it would shrink. Where do they go, and what makes them go?

The half of the loop nobody has explained yet

Every lesson in this block has followed the arrival side. Lesson 06 gave the Wnt gradient a cell reads to know how far up it is. Lesson 07 gave the integrins holding it to the basement membrane, the junctions holding it to its neighbours, and the climb itself at around 4 micrometres an hour. Lesson 08 gives the division at the base that supplies every cell making the journey.

Departure has been mentioned in nearly all of them and explained in none. Lesson 01 said worn cells are shed into the lumen. Lesson 04 said a phosphatidylserine molecule appearing on the outer surface of a dying cell is read by macrophages as an instruction to engulf it, and then handed the control of that removal to this lesson. Lesson 07 said cells are shed at the surface, used the word extruded once, and defined it nowhere.

Here is the loop those pieces belong to.

Read the closing link twice. It runs from loss back to production, which is the direction that makes the arrangement stable. A tissue that renews itself this fast is a tissue whose disposal has to work as reliably as its manufacture, and there is no version of the loop where only one half matters.

What this lesson has to establish

Three questions, in order.

First, what actually removes a cell at the top? The answer is a programme the cell runs on itself, and running it tidily matters enormously to a sheet whose whole job is to stay sealed.

Second, what tells that cell to run the programme? Part of the answer is where the cell is. An epithelial cell that loses its grip on the matrix beneath it dies, and that turns out to be a rule the tissue depends on.

Third, and this is the one worth staying for: what happens when the climb stops ending? Not what happens to one cell. What happens to a tissue that keeps making cells at the base while removal at the top has stopped working. Colorectal cancer is the clinical form of that failure, and lesson 01 promised that this block would close where it opened, on the same structure, from the other side.

There is also a fourth possibility the loop does not show, and it is the one most accounts of this material get wrong. A cell can stop dividing permanently and stay in the tissue, alive, doing things. That is neither division nor death, it has consequences in both directions, and it gets a scene of its own.

Check
id check-prerequisites

Before going on, retrieve three things from earlier in the block. Answer each in a sentence, then compare.

  1. In lesson 06, what does a colonic crypt cell use to work out how far it is from the base, and which direction does that quantity run?
  2. In lesson 07, what holds the base of a crypt cell to the matrix underneath the sheet?
  3. If a crypt makes about 175 cells a day and holds about 700, what must be true of the rate at which cells leave?

Answers. First: Wnt signalling, which is highest at the crypt base and decreases progressively up the crypt axis, so a cell reads its height from how much Wnt signal it is receiving. Second: integrins, binding the laminins and fibronectin of the basement membrane, with integrin-linked kinase joining the integrin beta1 tail to actin inside the cell. Third: it must also be about 175 cells a day, averaged over time. Any sustained mismatch changes the number of cells in the crypt, in one direction or the other.

If the first two did not come back, the lesson is still followable and will simply be harder work. The recovery route in scene 7 says exactly which scenes of lessons 06 and 07 to reread and what to take from each.

Callout
id callout-borrowed-cycle-vocabulary

This lesson borrows one thing from the cell cycle and does not teach it: that the cycle contains points where a cell can be held back, and that a cell with damaged DNA can be arrested at one of those points long enough to repair its genome before continuing. That is the whole of the checkpoint account this lesson's argument requires.

Lesson 08 of this block (PREM-05.08) owns the cell cycle, mitosis, chromosome segregation and the checkpoints, and owns stem-cell renewal in the crypt. Everything this lesson says about checkpoints is the minimum its own argument needs, sourced here independently, and nothing in it should be read as a summary of that lesson. Where you want the machinery, that is where it lives.

Callout
id callout-lesson-boundary

The last third of this lesson is about cancer, and colorectal cancer specifically, because that is the disease this block's structure produces when its control fails. Everything here is a teaching example and not medical advice. The lesson states no diagnosis, no prognosis, no treatment, no screening recommendation and no personal risk, and the population figures it quotes describe studied groups and say nothing about any reader. Clinical oncology management is outside this course's scope by design and is not discussed.

scenes.title: A cell that takes itself apart
scenes.contentHtml:
A cell that takes itself apart

Two cells die in a tissue section. The first has swollen, its plasma membrane has given way, and its contents have gone out into the space around it. Neighbouring cells look normal; a rim of inflammatory cells has arrived. The second has shrunk, its chromatin has condensed, and it has broken into several compact fragments, each one still wrapped in intact membrane. There is no inflammatory rim. A neighbouring epithelial cell has already engulfed two of the fragments.

Both cells are dead. Almost nothing else about them is the same, and the difference is not the amount of damage. The second cell did that to itself.

The observation that named it

In 1972 Kerr, Wyllie and Currie collected these tidy deaths from a range of tissues and argued that they were one phenomenon. They proposed the name apoptosis for a mechanism of controlled cell deletion, and made a claim about what it is for: it plays a complementary but opposite role to mitosis in regulating animal cell populations.

Set that beside the loop from scene 1. Mitosis at the base, apoptosis at the top, and a cell number that stays constant because the two are matched. The 1972 paper reached that reading from morphology alone, meaning from what the cells looked like under a microscope and nothing else, and it holds.

The structural changes they described come in two stages. First the nucleus and cytoplasm condense and the cell breaks into a number of membrane-bound fragments whose internal structure is still well preserved. Then those fragments, which they called apoptotic bodies, are either shed from epithelial-lined surfaces or taken up by other cells. They read the morphology as evidence of an active, inherently programmed process, one that environmental stimuli can start or hold off, and they reported it in the ordinary turnover of many healthy adult tissues.

Notice the phrase shed from epithelial-lined surfaces. The crypt is an epithelial-lined surface, and one of the two disposal routes in the original description is the one this block has been calling shedding since lesson 01.

Definition
id definition-apoptosis

Apoptosis is a form of cell death that the dying cell carries out itself, using machinery it already contains, with a characteristic result: the cell condenses, breaks into membrane-bounded fragments, keeps its contents inside them, and is cleared by neighbouring or phagocytic cells without provoking an inflammatory response.

The word names a programme, not a degree of injury. A cell running it has not been overwhelmed; it has been switched on.

Why the tidiness is the point, not a detail

The colonic epithelium is one cell thick, and its job is to keep the lumen on the lumen side. Now put the two death styles into it.

An apoptotic cell keeps its plasma membrane intact even late in its disassembly, so its cytoplasmic contents are not released into the interstitium. It is cleared quickly, and there is essentially no inflammatory reaction associated with the process. The cell that has lost membrane integrity does the opposite: its contents go out into the surrounding tissue, chemotactic signals follow, inflammatory cells are recruited, and inflammation is usually present.

That second outcome is manageable as an occasional accident. As a routine disposal method it would not be. Around 175 cells a day leave one crypt, and a tissue disposing of them by spilling their contents under a sheet that has to stay sealed would be running a permanent inflammatory response as the price of ordinary maintenance. Whether the tissue could tolerate that is not something this lesson has measured, and the reasoning here is the lesson's own and not a quoted finding. What the sources establish is narrower and enough: the tidy route exists, it is the one the tissue uses for turnover, and it does not provoke inflammation.

Lesson 04 already gave you the signal that makes the clearance work. Phosphatidylserine is normally held on the cytoplasmic side of the plasma membrane. On an apoptotic cell it appears on the outer surface, where it is a recognition ligand for phagocytes. A molecule the outside world never sees becomes visible, and that visibility is the message. The cell does not merely die neatly; it labels itself for collection.

How much machinery you actually need

Enough of the machinery to reason with, and no more. The syllabus for this module excludes memorising every signalling intermediate, and this is the place that exclusion bites hardest.

Apoptosis is a coordinated and often energy-dependent process that runs through a family of proteases called caspases. They divide into two functional groups: initiators, which respond to the signal that starts the process, and executioners, which do the disassembly. Two routes reach them. An extrinsic route starts at death receptors in the plasma membrane, which belong to the tumour necrosis factor receptor family, so the signal to die can arrive from outside the cell. An intrinsic route starts inside, at the mitochondrion, which releases proteins from its intermembrane space into the cytosol; cytochrome c is one of them, and it assembles with Apaf-1 and procaspase-9 into a complex called the apoptosome. Both routes converge on the executioners. Once caspases are activated there seems to be an irreversible commitment, and the whole process can be over in two to three hours.

What to hold: two routes, one from outside and one from inside, converging on a shared execution step that runs quickly and does not reverse. What not to hold: the numbering. Which caspase carries which number is a lookup, and no question in this lesson turns on it.

The word "necrosis" is doing less work than it looks

Here the vocabulary needs care, because the clean pairing of apoptosis against necrosis is a simplification and the field has retired it.

The Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death draws its main line somewhere else: between accidental cell death, the immediate and catastrophic end of a cell exposed to a severe physical, chemical or mechanical insult, and regulated cell death, which relies on dedicated molecular machinery and can therefore be delayed or accelerated by a genetic or pharmacological intervention. Programmed cell death, in the committee's usage, names the regulated forms that run in ordinary physiology without any outside perturbation. And the committee deliberately classifies death on genetic, biochemical, pharmacological and functional grounds instead of on how the cell looks, because there are regulated pathways whose end result looks necrotic. Necroptosis and pyroptosis are two.

So "necrosis" describes an appearance: a cell that swelled and burst. It does not by itself tell you whether machinery was running. The contrast that survives is between a death the cell executed and a death that happened to it, and that contrast is testable, because you can interfere with machinery and see the death change.

Check
id check-programme-not-damage

A researcher applies a compound that blocks caspase activity to a monolayer of epithelial cells, then applies a stimulus that normally kills them. Cell death is delayed by several hours.

Two questions. What does that result establish about the death being studied? And would the same experiment distinguish accidental cell death from a regulated pathway with a necrotic appearance?

Answers. First, it establishes that the death depends on machinery the cell contains, because interfering with one component changed the timing. That is the defining property of regulated cell death, and it is why the committee draws its line at machinery and not at appearance. It does not on its own establish that the pathway is apoptosis, since caspases participate in more than one regulated route.

Second, it would separate accidental death from regulated death, because accidental death by definition does not depend on a dedicated pathway and so a caspase inhibitor should not delay it. It would not reliably separate apoptosis from a regulated pathway that ends up looking necrotic; for that you need the biochemical and genetic evidence the committee's scheme is built on, and appearance in a section is not enough.

scenes.title: Attachment as permission to stay alive
scenes.contentHtml:
Attachment as permission to stay alive

Lesson 07 was firm about one thing. An enterocyte never leaves the sheet. It stays joined to its neighbours by every attachment in its junctional map for the whole journey up the crypt, and it is shed only at the end of that journey. There is no free leading edge, no crawling, no turning around.

Which raises a question lesson 07 did not answer. If the cell is held on the whole way, what makes the end the end?

An experiment on cells that had nowhere to sit

In 1994 Frisch and Francis took epithelial cells, the MDCK line derived from dog kidney, and disrupted the interactions between them and the extracellular matrix. The cells died, and they died by apoptosis. The authors named the phenomenon anoikis, from the Greek for homelessness.

Read what that result says. These cells were not injured, starved or poisoned. They were denied a surface to attach to. Attachment was supplying something the cell needed in order to keep running, and removing it started the programme from scene 2.

Definition
id definition-anoikis

Anoikis is apoptosis triggered by the loss of, or by inappropriate, attachment between a cell and the extracellular matrix. It is the same execution machinery described in scene 2, reached by a different starting condition: a cell finds itself somewhere it should not be, and the response is to run the programme.

The name is Greek for homelessness, which is unusually apt. What the cell has lost is not a nutrient or a signal from another cell. It has lost its address.

Two details from the 1994 work matter more than the headline. First, sensitivity was regulated rather than universal: anoikis did not occur in normal fibroblasts, so this is a property of some cell types and not a general consequence of floating free. Second, it could be switched off. Two of the interventions that switched it off used oncogenes, which are genes whose activation contributes to a cell's growth advantage; putting one into a cell and changing how the cell grows is what transformation means here. Introducing either of two such genes, v-Ha-ras or v-src, abolished anoikis in epithelial cells. So did a chemical treatment with a phorbol ester, and so did making the cell produce extra quantities of a protein called bcl-2. The authors suggested that getting around anoikis accompanies the acquisition of anchorage independence, meaning the ability to grow without a surface to sit on, or of motility. A later review adds the reason anyone cares: losing anoikis is thought to make it easier for cells to survive away from where they started and settle somewhere else, which is what metastasis means.

Hold that second point. A cell that survives detachment is doing something the experiment says takes a specific change to achieve.

Scope the finding honestly before carrying it anywhere. This is a cell line in culture, from dog kidney, in 1994, with attachment removed abruptly by the experimenter. It establishes that epithelial survival can be attachment-dependent and that the dependence can be broken. It does not by itself establish what happens at the top of a human colonic crypt.

What the crypt actually supplies, and what it does not

Lesson 07 gave you the attachment in question. Epithelial cells of the human intestinal crypt bind a basement membrane of laminins and fibronectin through integrins, with integrin-linked kinase joining the integrin beta1 tail to actin inside the cell. That is the grip whose loss anoikis responds to, in the tissue this block follows.

And the connection is not this lesson's guess. The same review of the human intestinal crypt states that cell survival is tightly regulated by RGD-dependent interactions between matrix and integrins, and that integrin receptors including alpha5beta1 and the alphaV integrins have a central role in controlling anoikis, meaning apoptosis on loss of attachment. So attachment-dependent survival is documented in this tissue and not only in a dog kidney line, and the receptors doing it are the ones lesson 07 already put at the base of the cell.

Now the honest part, and it is the most important paragraph in the scene.

The best-studied version of shedding in the intestine is at the tip of a small-intestinal villus, where cells are lost from a region called the extrusion zone. A 2015 review of that process states plainly that it is not known whether cell death precedes the start of detachment or whether detachment itself causes the death, the second of those being anoikis. The same review reports evidence pointing the other way, that the apoptotic pathway appears to be activated before cells reach the extrusion zone at all.

So the order of events is open. Both stories are live: a cell might detach and then die, or die and then be pushed out. This lesson is not going to close that question, and neither should you when you meet it in an exam or a paper. Anoikis is established as a real phenomenon and a real capability of epithelial cells. Anoikis as the trigger for shedding at an intestinal surface is a candidate mechanism with contrary evidence beside it.

The mechanics of the removal itself are better settled. Tight junction protein ZO-1 redistributes about fifteen minutes before a cell is shed, and after the cell leaves, the gap it opens is sealed by neighbours re-forming tight junctions within about twenty minutes. The sheet closes behind the departing cell. Barrier and disposal are solved together, which is what a one-cell-thick lining has to do.

One number, carefully scoped: an estimated 1400 mature enterocytes are shed from a single small-intestinal villus tip every 24 hours. That is a small-intestinal measurement from a review about small-intestinal villi, and this lesson does not carry it over to the colon, whose surface is arranged differently. Use it for the sense of scale it gives and nothing more.

The tissue decides, and crowding is how

Here is the finding that shifts the whole account, and it is why this scene is where the phrase tissue context first earns its place.

Epithelia extrude cells in response to crowding. When a monolayer becomes too dense, cells leave, and the number comes back down. In 2012 Eisenhoffer and colleagues showed that most of the cells leaving this way were still alive when they left: they were caspase-negative in 80 per cent of extrusions from human colon sections, 88 per cent in zebrafish epidermis and 67 per cent in cultured monolayers. Crowding was doing the selecting, and a stretch-activated ion channel, Piezo1, was required. Block the stretch-activated channels with gadolinium, or knock Piezo1 down in zebrafish, and extrusion falls off.

Definition
id definition-extrusion

Extrusion is the squeezing of a single cell out of an epithelial sheet by its neighbours, which close the gap behind it. Lesson 07 used the word once without defining it; this is the sense meant. Extrusion is a mechanical removal, and it is separable from death: a cell may be dead before it goes, or alive as it goes and die afterwards.

The order of cause and effect flips in this account. In anoikis as usually pictured, a cell loses attachment and therefore dies. In crowding-induced extrusion, the tissue removes a living cell because there are too many cells, and the cell then dies because it is outside. The authors' own reading is that most extruded cells die from anoikis after the fact, from loss of survival signals from the matrix they no longer touch. They present that as the likely outcome rather than something they demonstrated in the animal, and the honest summary is that the mechanical step is established and the death that follows it is inferred.

What is established is enough to change how you think about the loop. Removal is not a private decision by a worn-out cell. It is a property of the sheet, responding to how many cells the sheet is carrying. Position and density decide who leaves. Nothing about the cell's genome has entered the story yet.

What blocking removal did

The last part of the 2012 result is the bridge to the rest of the lesson. When extrusion was blocked, cells did not simply stay put and behave. Zebrafish treated with gadolinium developed epidermal cell masses at the fin edges, and Piezo1 morphants developed the same masses at fin edges and other sites of tissue strain. Cell density stayed elevated where control tissue's density had recovered.

The authors go one step further and suggest that such masses may set the stage for tumourigenesis by allowing defective cells to be retained, noting that colon polyp sections showed increased cell density and no clearly identified extrusions compared with control sections. Weigh that carefully. The masses in zebrafish are a demonstrated consequence of blocking extrusion. The link to tumour formation in a human colon is a suggestion supported by a difference between polyp and control sections, which is an association in tissue examined once. It is a reasonable hypothesis and it is not a demonstrated causal chain, and the paper says as much.

Check
id check-detachment-survivor

A cultured epithelial cell line is detached from its substrate and kept in suspension. Most cells die within hours. One subpopulation survives, divides in suspension, and forms colonies.

What has that subpopulation lost, in the terms of this scene? And name one thing this observation does not establish about it.

Answers. It has lost anoikis: the attachment-dependence of its own survival. Detachment is no longer sufficient to start the programme in these cells, which is exactly what the 1994 work produced deliberately by transforming epithelial cells with v-Ha-ras or v-src, and what overexpressed bcl-2 also achieved.

What it does not establish: that these cells would form a tumour, or spread to another site, in an animal or a person. Surviving in suspension is one capability. The 1994 authors put it as circumvention of anoikis accompanying anchorage independence or motility, and a later review puts the metastasis connection as something anoikis loss is thought to facilitate. Both are careful with the verb, and so should you be. Growing in a flask without a floor is a long way short of a disease.

scenes.title: The cells that stop and stay
scenes.contentHtml:
The cells that stop and stay

The loop in scene 1 offers a cell two futures. Divide, or be removed. There is a third, and it is not on the diagram because it is not part of the loop: stop dividing permanently and stay where you are, alive.

That state has a name, it is common, and almost everything a learner arrives believing about it is wrong.

What senescence is

Definition
id definition-senescence

Cellular senescence is an essentially irreversible arrest of cell proliferation, entered when a cell experiences stress of a kind that could otherwise make it cancerous. A senescent cell stays viable and metabolically active. It has stopped dividing and it has not been removed.

Three parts of that definition need separating out, because each one contradicts a common assumption.

Essentially irreversible. You already know from lesson 01 that not dividing and being unable to divide are different things: the definition of a stem cell given there was about capacity rather than current activity, and a quiescent stem cell can be activated. Senescence is the other case. The arrest is a durable one, and its permanence is the property that makes the rest of the story work.

Viable and metabolically active. The cell is not dying, not shrinking, not being cleared. It is present, running its metabolism, and as the next section shows, secreting.

Stress that could make it cancerous. This is the part that dismantles "senescent means old". The triggers are damage and inappropriate signalling: telomere shortening that leaves the telomeres unable to do their job, breaks through both strands of the DNA, activation of an oncogene, disturbance of the epigenome, and too much mitogenic signalling.

Three of those names belong to machinery this lesson does not own, and it is parking them rather than teaching them. A telomere is part of a chromosome's structure; the epigenome is the set of chemical marks on DNA and its packaging that help set which genes a cell reads; a mitogenic signal is one whose message is to divide. Take those as vocabulary at dictionary level, because nothing in this lesson turns on their detail, and expect the chromosome and cell-cycle material to be where they are properly developed.

What the list is for is its shape. Every entry is either damage or a wrong signal. Telomere shortening is one item among five, and it is the one that made everyone think the word senescence meant elapsed time. The category is defined by the trigger being oncogenic stress, not by the cell having been around a long while.

Take the oncogene entry seriously, because it is the cleanest result in the field. Switch on an oncogene in a cell and the cell may respond by arresting permanently. The change that ought to make it divide without limit instead stops it dividing at all. This is called oncogene-induced senescence, and it means a cell has a response available to a dangerous mutation that neither divides nor dies.

What it buys

The permanence is the point. A cell that has sustained oncogenic stress and can never divide again cannot found a growing population, whatever else is wrong with it. That is why the senescence response is read as having evolved at least partly to suppress the development of cancer, and why it acts as a strong constraint on the formation of malignant tumours.

One word in that sentence needs marking. Malignant is the source's word and it does specific work: it separates growths that stay where they arose from those that do not. What makes a growth capable of leaving its site of origin is not this lesson's material, and the lesson uses the word as a label without unpacking it.

Put it beside scene 2 and you have two different solutions to the same problem. A cell that must not be allowed to divide can be removed from the tissue by apoptosis, or held in the tissue permanently arrested by senescence. Both stop the lineage. They leave the tissue in different states, and that difference is where the trouble starts.

What it costs

A senescent cell is still there, and it is not quiet. Senescent cells display what is called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype: they secrete numerous proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, growth factors and proteases into the tissue around them.

That secretion is the mechanism behind the second half of the account. Senescence may act as a basic ageing process that drives ageing phenotypes and age-related pathology later in life. And the secretions can go the other way on cancer too: by sustaining chronic inflammation and making the local environment permissive, the same secretory phenotype that follows from a cancer-suppressing arrest can promote the development of cancer.

Read that last sentence again, because it is not a contradiction to be resolved. The same response, in the same cell, in the same tissue, both constrains tumours and can encourage them, depending on when in a life it happens and what else is present.

Do not tidy this up

The framework for holding two opposed effects of one mechanism is antagonistic pleiotropy: a trait selected for its benefit at one stage of life carries costs at another, and selection is weaker on late-life costs. Senescence fits it. Arresting a damaged cell early in life prevents a growing population of damaged cells; the same arrested cells accumulating and secreting across decades contribute to age-related pathology.

So resist three tidy statements, all of which you will meet.

"Senescence is what happens to old cells." No: it is a response to oncogenic stress, and elapsed time is not its definition.

"Senescence is a failure of the cell." No: it is a functioning response with a demonstrated protective role, which is why it is described as having evolved for that purpose.

"Senescence is good, or senescence is bad." Neither, and the field does not claim either. It is a mechanism with effects in both directions, and the honest position is to say which effect you are talking about and over what timescale.

A learner who can hold that shape will handle the rest of this lesson, because cancer has the same shape. One change, several possible consequences, decided by context.

Check
id check-three-fates

A colonic crypt cell sustains DNA damage severe enough that it must not divide again. Three routes are available: apoptosis, senescence, or continuing to divide.

Describe what the tissue is left holding in each case, and say which of the three leaves a cell in the tissue that is secreting into it.

Answers. With apoptosis, the tissue is left holding nothing from that cell. It condenses, breaks into membrane-bounded fragments, is cleared by neighbours or shed from the surface, and provokes no inflammatory response. The lineage ends and the cell is gone.

With senescence, the tissue is left holding a living, metabolically active cell that will never divide again and that secretes proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, growth factors and proteases into its surroundings. The lineage ends and the cell stays. This is the route that leaves a secreting cell in the tissue.

With continued division, the tissue is left holding a growing population of cells carrying the damage. The lineage does not end, and the number of cells in the crypt begins to depart from the balance scene 1 established.

The comparison is worth making because the first two are both successful outcomes for the tissue in the short term and they are not equivalent in the long term. A tissue that solves every dangerous cell by senescence accumulates secreting cells; one that solves them all by apoptosis has to replace them.

scenes.title: Working out how badly the loop has to fail
scenes.contentHtml:
Working out how badly the loop has to fail

Most accounts of cancer start with a list. This one starts with the arithmetic from scene 1, because the arithmetic answers a question the list cannot: how large does the failure have to be?

The intuition almost everyone brings is that a tumour needs a dramatic breakdown, cells dividing wildly, control collapsing. Work the numbers and that intuition does not survive.

One relationship carries the whole calculation. Write the crypt as a single population of size NN, with cells entering at a production rate PP and leaving at a loss rate LL, both in cells per day. The population then changes at whatever rate the two fail to match:

In words: the number of cells in a crypt rises exactly as fast as production exceeds loss, and holds steady only while the two are equal. Scene 1 stated that as a sentence. This is the same statement written so it can be used.

Worked Example
id worked-example-how-small-a-mismatch

The task. A crypt holds about 700 cells and produces about 175 a day. Suppose removal at the top falls slightly behind production and stays behind. How small can that shortfall be and still change the tissue over a human lifetime?

Step 1: write down what is given, and in what units.

Population of one crypt, N, about 700 cells. Production rate, P, about 175 cells per day. For the balance in scene 1 to hold, the loss rate L must also be about 175 cells per day. Every quantity is a rate in cells per day except N, which is a count.

Step 2: choose the model and say why it fits.

Use the balance relation stated above, that the rate of change of the population equals production minus loss. It fits because scene 1 established the balance as a statement about rates and not about individual cells, and because every source figure available here is a population figure. It is the simplest model that can answer the question, which is the reason to start with it.

Step 3: make the shortfall concrete.

Let removal fall behind production by one per cent. Then L is 0.99 P, so:

dN/dt = P - 0.99P = 0.01P = 0.01 x 175 = 1.75 cells per day.

One and three-quarter extra cells a day. In a structure holding 700. That is a shortfall no measurement of a single crypt would notice.

Step 4: run it forward, and check the arithmetic independently.

Time to accumulate an extra 700 cells, doubling the crypt's population:

t = 700 / 1.75 = 400 days.

Check it the other way to make sure the division went the right way up: 1.75 cells per day x 400 days = 700 cells. It agrees. Just over a year, from a one per cent mismatch.

Step 5: state the assumption that is doing the most work, and which way it errs.

This treats the accumulating cells as inert, contributing nothing to production. That is almost certainly wrong: if the retained cells divide like the rest, production rises as the population rises, and growth becomes exponential instead of steady. So 400 days is an estimate under a fixed rate, and the real behaviour of such a population could differ in either direction. The model is an illustration, not a forecast, and it is worth being exact about why rather than calling it a floor.

Calling it a floor would assume the retained cells divide, and that further divisions only add. Neither is safe. A retained cell may not divide at all. And as cells accumulate, production, extrusion, differentiation, death and the geometry of the space all change with density, which can accelerate the accumulation, slow it, stop it, or reverse it. So the arithmetic shows what a small persistent mismatch is capable of over a year. It does not predict what a real crypt would do.

Two further limits. The figure of 175 cells a day is itself lesson 01's steady-state estimate rather than a measurement of one crypt. And a real crypt is not a well-mixed population; its cells occupy positions, which is precisely what the rest of this lesson is about. The model deliberately ignores position in order to isolate the rate question.

Step 6: interpret the result in its original context.

The answer is that the failure does not have to be dramatic. It has to be persistent. A one per cent standing mismatch, invisible in any single snapshot, is enough to change a structure over about a year at that fixed rate. What a real crypt would do depends on how its rates respond to the crowding, which this model sets aside.

Now put that beside what the cancer genomics says about time. Developing a full-blown metastatic cancer takes decades. A colorectal tumour in a 90-year-old patient carries nearly twice as many mutations as a tumour in a 45-year-old that looks identical under a microscope. The genomic account and the arithmetic account point at the same shape: a small, sustained, cumulative departure from balance running over a very long time.

Step 7: the self-explanation prompt. Which single decision in this worked example most determines the answer? Write your answer before reading on.

It is the decision in step 2 to model the crypt as rates instead of as cells. Once the question is "how do two rates compare", a one per cent difference is obviously enough given a long enough run, and the size of the daily number stops mattering. Had the example started from individual cells and their fates, the same conclusion would have needed far more machinery to reach.

Three places the mismatch can come from

The loop gives exactly three ways for loss to fall behind production, and it is worth naming them separately because they are different biology.

Production rises. More cells are made per day at the base than before.

The climb stops ending. Cells that should have stopped dividing on the way up keep dividing. Nothing is wrong with removal at the top; the population arriving there is simply too large, and cells that should have differentiated and become a departing enterocyte remain proliferative instead.

Removal fails. Cells reach the top and are not taken out of the sheet. This is the failure scenes 2 and 3 make available: the apoptotic programme not running, or attachment-dependence lost so that detachment no longer starts it, or extrusion not happening when the sheet gets crowded.

These are not alternatives to each other. A tissue can suffer more than one, and the second and third are hard to distinguish by looking at a section, which the next scene will make use of.

The joint lesson 06 identified

Lesson 06 of this block did the hardest part of this already, and it stopped precisely where this lesson takes over.

Its result was about reading position. About 93 per cent of colorectal cancers carry an activating mutation in the Wnt pathway, and the gene most often affected is APC. APC is a component of the destruction complex, and it is also required for that complex to reorient towards a Wnt cue. A cell with damaged APC accumulates beta-catenin and runs the beta-catenin-dependent gene programme whether or not Wnt is present. Lesson 06's summary of the consequence: the gradient outside the cell is unchanged, and the cell now reports that it is at the crypt base at every height.

Take that sentence into this lesson's loop and the second failure follows immediately. The gene programme a crypt-base cell runs is the programme of a dividing, undifferentiated cell. A cell running it at every height keeps dividing at every height and never completes the differentiation that ends the climb. The climb stops ending, in the most literal sense available: the signal that would have ended it is being read as its opposite.

Nothing about removal has broken in that account. The cell has simply never become the kind of cell that leaves.

Colorectal cancer is described as following a stepwise progression from normal epithelium through characterised mutations to a carcinoma. The intermediate stage is called an adenoma, and the sequence is named after the two of them: the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence. Those two words are stage names from pathology and this lesson uses them as labels, at the level of adenoma being the earlier and benign stage and carcinoma the later one; what distinguishes them under a microscope is not this lesson's material.

APC is usually where that sequence starts in the colon. The literature calls the first mutation in such a sequence a gatekeeping one, and in the colon it most often occurs in APC, with mutations in KRAS and other genes following.

Where checkpoints come in, and how little this lesson needs from them

The lesson's outcome asks for failed checkpoints as well, and here is the minimum required.

A cell with damaged DNA can be held back in the cycle long enough to repair its genome before continuing. p53 is the protein most associated with that hold. It is a stress sensor that responds to DNA damage, to hyperproliferative signalling and to several other stresses, and it can produce three outcomes: transient arrest, permanent arrest as senescence, or apoptosis. TP53, the gene encoding it, is inactivated in more than half of all sporadic human cancers.

So one protein sits at the junction of all three scenes so far. It can arrest a cell, it can send it into the senescence of scene 4, and it can start the apoptosis of scene 2. Losing it removes an input to all three at once, which is a large part of why its loss is so common in cancers.

Be careful about what follows from that, because the field is careful. The downstream genes and pathways that matter for p53's tumour suppression remain unresolved, and depending on the tissue either the cell-cycle arrest function or the apoptosis function can be the one that matters. Which of p53's three responses does the tumour-suppressing work is not a settled question, and a lesson that told you it was would be teaching you something false.

Lesson 08 of this block owns the cell cycle and its checkpoints, and the account above is deliberately the smallest one this lesson's argument needs. What this lesson supplies is the other end: what the arrested or damaged cell does next, and what the tissue does about it.

scenes.title: One mutation, several possible outcomes
scenes.contentHtml:
One mutation, several possible outcomes

Commit to an answer before reading on, and write it down so you can check it against yourself later.

A patch of ordinary, healthy-looking skin is sampled from a middle-aged adult and sequenced deeply. What fraction of its cells would you expect to carry a mutation in a gene that drives cancers when it is mutated in a tumour? Give a number.

Most people answer with something very small. A fraction of a per cent, perhaps. Something rare enough that finding one would be notable.

The model that produces that answer

Misconception
id misconception-mutation-equals-cancer

The model. A cancer is a mutated cell that has multiplied. Mutations in cancer genes are therefore rare in healthy tissue, because a cell that acquires one becomes a cancer cell, and cancer is uncommon. On this account the disease lives in the genome: identify the mutations, and you have identified the cancer. Tissue is the place it happens, and the interesting causation is all inside the cell.

This is a reasonable model to hold. It is what a list of cancer genes implies, it explains why mutation-causing exposures raise cancer rates, and every part of it that concerns mutation is correct. Mutations in driver genes really are what start the process.

What it cannot explain. In 2015 Martincorena and colleagues sequenced 234 small biopsies of sun-exposed eyelid epidermis from four donors aged 55 to 73. The skin was normal epidermis free of visible lesions, and it was doing its job.

Mutations in NOTCH1 were present in 14 to 21 per cent of skin cells. NOTCH2 in 5 to 7 per cent, NOTCH3 in 2 to 3 per cent. Taken together, about a quarter of all skin cells in those biopsies carried a NOTCH mutation. TP53 and FAT1 mutations were each in 3 to 5 per cent of cells. On average each normal cell carried 0.27 driver point mutations, with a 95 per cent confidence interval from 0.19 to 0.35. The authors' summary is that aged, sun-exposed skin is a patchwork of thousands of evolving clones, with over a quarter of its cells carrying mutations of the kind found in cancers while the epidermis goes on maintaining its physiological functions.

These were not early cancers found by looking hard. The mutations were under positive selection, meaning the statistics showed the mutated cells were doing better than their neighbours instead of drifting along by chance. Each patch of descendants of one such cell is a clone, and those clones had expanded. And the tissue was working throughout. Some clones carried two or three driver mutations and had still not acquired malignant potential, which led the authors to ask what combinations of events are actually sufficient for transformation.

The first model has no room for this result. If a driver mutation made a cell a cancer cell, a quarter of that epidermis would have been cancer, and it was not.

The more adequate model. A driver mutation is necessary and it is not sufficient. What happens to a cell carrying one is decided by the mutation together with the state of the tissue it is sitting in: what its neighbours are doing, whether it is still attached where it should be, how crowded the sheet is, and which of the available responses that particular tissue reaches for. The mutation sets what is possible. The tissue decides much of what actually occurs.

Comparing the two models on the same case. Take one epidermal cell with a NOTCH1 mutation, in the eyelid skin above.

The first model predicts a cancer cell, and a tissue containing a great many of them. It cannot then explain the intact epidermis, and it has no way to describe the difference between this cell and one in a tumour, because on its account they are the same cell.

The second model predicts what was found. A cell with a growth advantage relative to its neighbours founds a clone, that clone expands, and it stays inside a functioning epithelium because the other controls have not failed: the cells are still attached, still responsive to crowding, still able to run the death programme, still able to arrest. The difference between this clone and a tumour is a difference in how many of those controls are intact, not in whether a mutation is present.

What "tissue context" actually consists of

The phrase is easy to say and easy to leave vague. This lesson has been building its content for four scenes, and it comes to three specific things, none of which is written in the cell's genome.

Whether the cell is where it belongs. Scene 3: epithelial survival can depend on attachment to the matrix, and a cell that loses that attachment can run the apoptotic programme. Position is a survival condition. Two cells with identical genomes, one attached and one not, are not in the same situation.

How many cells the sheet is carrying. Scene 3 again: crowding drives extrusion, and in the 2012 work most cells extruded during ordinary homeostasis were still alive when they left. A sheet at normal density and the same sheet when crowded do different things to the same cell. The decision to remove is being made by mechanical state, and the cell being removed had no vote.

Which response the tissue reaches for. Scene 4 and scene 5 together: p53 can produce transient arrest, senescence or apoptosis, and depending on the tissue either its arrest function or its apoptosis function can be the one that matters for suppressing tumours. One protein, one kind of damage, and the response that does the work differs by tissue. That is not a gap in the knowledge waiting to be filled by a better list of genes. It is the finding.

Read the two outcomes in that map by comparing what feeds each one. Every arrow is a contribution, and both outcomes have more than one arrow arriving. The mutation is upstream of both, so it is not what tells them apart. What tells them apart is whether the tissue's own controls are still working.

How the numbers on both sides fit together

Two sets of figures now sit side by side, and they agree.

From normal tissue: an average of 0.27 driver point mutations per cell in normal skin, with individual clones carrying two or three and still not malignant.

From tumours: a typical tumour contains two to eight driver mutations, and in common adult tumours including colorectal cancer the number of mutated driver genes is often three to six. Of everything else in a tumour's genome, more than 99.9 per cent of the alterations are immaterial to the disease. In a common solid tumour of the colon, breast, brain or pancreas, an average of 33 to 66 genes carry mutations that would be expected to change their protein products, and only a few of those are drivers. The rest are passengers, conferring no growth advantage, carried along.

So the difference between a normal-looking clone and a tumour is a small number of additional drivers, accumulated over decades, in a tissue whose other controls have also given way. Not a bright line. A count, plus a context.

That is also why the failure analysis in scene 5 matters more than a list of mutations would. Two of its three failure modes concern removal and differentiation, and only the third concerns division, and those are exactly the controls that decide whether a mutated clone stays a clone.

Check
id check-recheck-new-case

Recheck the model on a case that is not skin.

A study sequences normal colonic crypts from adults with no known bowel disease and reports that some crypts carry mutations in genes recurrently mutated in colorectal cancer, in tissue that is histologically normal.

Two questions. Does this result surprise you, given this scene? And what would have to be shown in addition before anyone could say those crypts were on the way to becoming a tumour?

Answers. It should not surprise you. The skin result establishes that normal, functioning tissue can carry driver mutations under positive selection, and the model that replaced the first one predicts that this is a general feature of renewing tissues rather than a peculiarity of eyelid skin. Predicting the colonic case is a fair use of the model.

What would have to be shown: that the additional drivers a tumour needs have accumulated, since a typical tumour carries two to eight and normal cells average well under one; and that the tissue-level controls have failed too, which means evidence about attachment, about removal at the surface, and about whether the affected cells still respond to crowding. Mutation in a histologically normal crypt is one of those requirements and not the set. Note also that this check is testing whether you can extend a model, not reporting a measurement: the evidence quoted in this lesson is from skin, and this pack contains no colonic dataset of that kind.

If your prediction at the top of the scene was "a fraction of a per cent", say specifically which part of your model produced that number. It will almost always be the assumption that a driver mutation and a cancer cell are the same thing.

Callout
id callout-normal-tissue-boundary

A word on what the skin finding does and does not say, because it is easy to misread in either direction.

It is a study of 234 biopsies from four donors, all of sun-exposed eyelid skin, all aged 55 to 73. It describes what those tissues contained. It is a teaching example here and it is not a statement about any reader's tissue, it carries no personal risk figure, and nothing in it supports or discourages any screening, monitoring or clinical action. This lesson makes no recommendation of any kind. The reason the study appears is narrower: it is the clearest available demonstration that carrying a driver mutation and having a cancer are different states, which is a fact about biology and not advice about anyone.

scenes.title: Practice: work the balance, then say what you cannot tell
scenes.contentHtml:
Practice: work the balance, then say what you cannot tell

Three tasks, with the support falling away. Attempt each one before reading its answer, and for the last one write your uncertainty down as part of the answer, where it belongs.

Task 1, with the steps supplied

A crypt holds about 700 cells and produces about 175 a day. Suppose the shortfall in removal is much smaller than the one per cent used in scene 5, and the crypt's population takes ten years to double instead of a little over a year.

Step 1. Convert ten years to days.

Step 2. Work out how many extra cells per day accumulate if 700 extra cells arrive over that period.

Step 3. Express that daily excess as a percentage of the 175 cells a day being produced.

Step 4. Say in one sentence what the number means for anyone trying to detect the imbalance.

Answers. Step 1: ten years is about 3650 days. Step 2: 700 cells divided by 3650 days is about 0.19 cells per day. Step 3: 0.19 divided by 175 is about 0.0011, so roughly 0.11 per cent, a little over one part in a thousand. Step 4: a mismatch of one part in a thousand between production and removal is enough to double a crypt's population within a decade, which means no measurement of production or removal accurate to a few per cent could distinguish a crypt in balance from one that is not.

Check the direction before moving on. A smaller shortfall gives a longer doubling time, and 0.11 per cent is smaller than the one per cent that gave 400 days. The two results are consistent.

Task 2, with less help

Three findings from three different tissue preparations. For each one, decide which of scene 5's three failure modes it points at, and name the mode.

Finding A. Cells in the upper part of a crypt are still expressing the gene programme characteristic of cells at the base, and are still dividing. Cells reaching the surface are being removed normally.

Finding B. An epithelial monolayer is crowded well past its normal density. Cell number does not come back down, and no extrusion events are seen.

Finding C. Detached epithelial cells recovered from a culture medium are alive, and a proportion of them go on to divide.

Answers. Finding A is the second failure mode: the climb stops ending. The population arriving at the top is too large because cells that should have stopped dividing and differentiated are still running the base programme, which is the consequence lesson 06 identified for a cell whose position reading has been decoupled. Removal is explicitly stated to be working.

Finding B is the third mode, removal failing, and specifically the extrusion route rather than the death programme. Crowding normally drives extrusion and brings cell number back down; here it does not.

Finding C is also the third mode, and also removal, but by a different route: these cells have lost the attachment-dependence of their survival, so detachment is no longer sufficient to start apoptosis. Distinguishing B from C matters because they are different repairs to the same imbalance, and because a section through a tissue would not tell them apart.

Task 3, unscaffolded

Two preparations of the same epithelium.

Preparation 1. Cell number is above normal. Apoptotic cells are present at the surface at the usual frequency, with condensed nuclei and intact membranes, and are being cleared without any inflammatory infiltrate.

Preparation 2. Cell number is above normal. Apoptotic cells are almost absent. Scattered cells have swollen and lost membrane integrity, and there is an inflammatory infiltrate.

Say for each preparation which controls appear to be operating and which do not, then state the two most important things neither description lets you decide.

Answer. Preparation 1: the apoptotic programme is operating and so is clearance, since the cells show the condensation and membrane integrity of scene 2 and are being removed without inflammation. So a failure of the death programme is the one explanation this description argues against.

Now resist finishing the sentence. It is tempting to conclude that the imbalance must therefore be on the production side, and the description does not license that, because it says nothing about the other removal route. Scene 3 established that extrusion is separable from death: a sheet can fail to extrude live cells when it becomes crowded while its apoptotic machinery works perfectly. Nothing here reports extrusion events at all. So preparation 1 is consistent with more cells being made, with cells failing to stop dividing on the climb, and with failed live-cell extrusion, and it separates none of the three.

Preparation 2: the apoptotic route is not visibly operating, and the cells that are dying are dying with membrane rupture and an inflammatory response, which is the accidental-appearing death of scene 2 and not the programme. So removal by apoptosis looks impaired here, and cell number is high, which is consistent.

The two things neither description settles. First, whether the raised cell number arose from increased production or from failed removal, in either preparation: a single snapshot of cell number and dying cells gives you a state and not a rate, and the whole argument of scene 5 was about rates. You would need the production rate and the loss rate, measured separately, to attribute the imbalance. Second, in preparation 2, whether the ruptured cells died accidentally or by a regulated pathway with a necrotic appearance. Scene 2's point was that appearance does not settle that question; you would need to interfere with the machinery and see whether the death changed.

If you did conclude "production side" for preparation 1, that is the most instructive wrong answer in this lesson, and it comes from treating apoptosis as the whole of removal. It is one of the two removal routes this lesson has described, and a sheet can lose the other one on its own.

If you wrote only the first of those two, that is the more important one and the answer is a good one. If you wrote neither and instead named a mutation, reread scene 6: none of these descriptions contains any information about a genome.

Accessibility and alternatives

Everything this lesson assesses can be done without seeing either diagram. Both carry a long description that states their nodes, every declared relationship, the direction of each one, and the conclusion the picture is meant to deliver, and the surrounding prose states the same relationships in sentences. The renewal loop is five stages joined in a closed ring, and its teaching point is a single relationship: the rate of loss sets the rate that must be replaced. The driver-mutation map is five ideas with two limiting links, and its teaching point is that the same mutation sits on both paths.

The arithmetic in scene 5 and in task 1 is worked in words and full sentences as well as in symbols, and the one displayed equation is read aloud in the prose immediately below it: the number of cells in a crypt rises exactly as fast as production exceeds loss. No result in this lesson depends on reading a figure, on colour, on position on a page, or on any interaction. No task asks a reader for any information about their own body, health, family history or tissue, and none ever will.

Recovery route

If this lesson has been hard going, the difficulty is almost always in one of three places, and each has a specific repair.

The loop and its arithmetic did not land. Reread scene 1 of this lesson, then lesson 01 of this block, scene "What seven hundred cells do that one cannot", which is where the 700 cells, the three-to-five-day renewal and the production-equals-loss statement were established. You need three things from it and nothing else: the cell count, the renewal interval, and the sentence that cells must leave at the same average rate they are made.

The position-reading argument in scene 5 did not land. Go to lesson 06 of this block, scenes 2 and 9. Scene 2 builds the destruction complex and how a signal arriving as an inhibitor of an inhibitor raises the output; scene 9 draws the consequence for a cell with damaged APC. If you take one sentence, take that lesson's own: the gradient outside the cell is unchanged, and what has broken is the reading.

The attachment argument in scene 3 did not land. Go to lesson 07 of this block, scene 4 for the junction map and the basal integrins, and scene 6 for the statement that an enterocyte never leaves the sheet and is shed only at the end of its journey. Anoikis is what makes that last clause do work: leaving the sheet and staying alive are ordinarily incompatible for this cell.

None of these is a prerequisite you were supposed to have memorised. Retrieving a fact you half-remember is a slower route to the same place, and taking it is not a sign that this lesson was too advanced.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: reading a growth without diagnosing anyone
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: reading a growth without diagnosing anyone

Callout
id callout-case-boundary

This case is a teaching example and not medical advice. The tissue description below is constructed for this lesson from features its sources establish; it is not a real specimen, a real report or a real person, and nothing in it is a diagnostic criterion. The scene carries no diagnosis, no prognosis, no staging, no treatment, no screening recommendation and no personal risk estimate. Clinical oncology management is outside this course's scope by design. What the scene shows is which conclusions this lesson's model licenses about a tissue, and which it does not.

A growth is removed from the wall of a colon and sectioned. The reasoning question is not what to call it. It is this: which parts of the renewal loop have failed here, which are still working, and what does the section refuse to tell you?

That question is answerable with this lesson and nothing else, which is the point of asking it.

Working the case

Worked Example
id worked-example-reading-the-growth

The description. A benign growth: an abnormal proliferation of cells, driven by at least one mutation. Compared with control colonic tissue, cell density is increased, and no extrusion events can be clearly identified. Proliferating cells are present well above the region where proliferation normally stops. The cells are still joined into an epithelium and still sitting on their basement membrane.

Step 1: locate the finding on the loop.

Cell density is up, so production has exceeded loss and stayed there. That is the whole content of the balance relation from scene 5: the population rises exactly as fast as production exceeds loss. The section tells you the imbalance happened. It does not tell you how fast, because a density is a state and the imbalance is a rate.

Step 2: which failure modes does the description implicate?

Two of scene 5's three, and they are visible separately here.

Proliferating cells above the normal proliferative region is the climb failing to end. Cells that should have stopped dividing and finished differentiating have not. That is what lesson 06 predicted for a cell whose position reading has been decoupled from the gradient: it runs the crypt-base programme at every height, and the crypt-base programme is the programme of a dividing, undifferentiated cell.

No clearly identifiable extrusion events, with density raised, is removal failing at the mechanical step. In control colonic tissue, extrusion is what brings density back down when a sheet becomes crowded. Here density is up and extrusion is not being seen.

Step 3: which controls are demonstrably still operating?

This step matters more than step 2 and is the one usually skipped.

The cells are still attached to the basement membrane and still joined into an epithelium. So the attachment-dependence of scene 3 has not been tested by this tissue, because nothing here has detached. Whether these cells could survive detachment is unknown from this description, and it is a different question from whether they are dividing too much.

The growth is confined and organised as an epithelium, which means the tissue-level constraints of scene 6 have not all given way. A clone can expand a long way inside a functioning epithelium. Scene 6's skin result is the reference case: about a quarter of the cells in normal eyelid epidermis carried NOTCH mutations, some clones carried two or three drivers, and the epidermis went on working.

Step 4: what the description does not settle, stated as a list because each item is a separate gap.

Whether the imbalance arose from raised production or from failed removal. Both are consistent with a raised density, and separating them needs the two rates measured, not a section.

Whether the apoptotic programme is intact. Nothing in the description reports apoptotic cells, their morphology, or their clearance. An absence of a report is not a report of absence.

How many driver mutations are present. A typical tumour carries two to eight, and common adult tumours of the colon often three to six, while normal cells average well under one. The description names at least one and stops there, and the difference between one and six is the difference the whole of scene 6 was about.

What will happen next. Progression from normal epithelium to carcinoma is described as stepwise and takes decades, and no single section establishes where along such a course any tissue sits, or that it will continue along it at all.

Step 5: what may be concluded.

That the imbalance is real, and that the differentiation control has given way, while attachment and epithelial organisation are still holding. That much is a genuine and useful reading, and it comes entirely from the loop.

Removal needs more care than that. A single fixed section cannot measure a rate. Extrusion is an event, so not seeing one in a section is consistent with a mechanism that has failed and equally consistent with one working too slowly to catch in a snapshot. The raised density is a reason to suspect removal is not keeping pace, and the reduced extrusion reported in colonic polyps is an association, which this lesson said when it introduced it. Showing that the removal control had failed would take a measurement over time, which this case does not have. So the reading is: one control demonstrably given way, one under suspicion, two still holding.

What may not be concluded is anything about a person. The reading describes a tissue's control state. It does not name a disease, predict a course, or bear on what anyone should do, and this lesson stops where that boundary is.

Step 6: the self-explanation prompt. Which step in this analysis would you have skipped if nobody had asked for it?

Almost everyone skips step 3. The trained instinct is to catalogue what has broken, and a tissue is more informative about its intact controls than about its broken ones, because the intact ones tell you which failures have not happened. Scene 6's whole argument depends on that asymmetry: a quarter of a normal epidermis carrying driver mutations is a fact about controls that were still working.

What the loop bought, and what it cost

Lesson 01 of this block opened with a question about architecture. Why is the lining of the colon built from an enormous number of small units instead of a few large ones?

This lesson supplies half of the answer that lesson could not give. A tissue made of small, individually replaceable units can be maintained by replacing units one at a time, continuously, without ever taking the sheet out of service. Removal is per cell. Manufacture is per cell. The barrier stays sealed throughout, because neighbours close the gap a departing cell leaves. The interval measured for that closing, about twenty minutes, comes from work on the small-intestinal villus tip rather than the colon, so read it as the order of magnitude for how fast the sealing is and not as a colonic figure.

The cost arrives with the benefit and is not separable from it. A tissue that maintains itself by continuous replacement is a tissue running division continuously, in one of the fastest-renewing structures the body has, for a lifetime. About 175 divisions a day per crypt, every day, for decades. Each of those divisions is an opportunity for the control on division to fail, and the arithmetic in scene 5 showed how small a standing failure has to be before it matters. Lesson 01's closing observation was that everything about the arrangement depends on division being started, stopped and positioned correctly over decades. This lesson is what that sentence means.

Colorectal cancer is the clinical form of that failure, and it is the reason this block opens and closes on the same structure.

What the block promised and what remains open

Five earlier lessons named this one. Each promise is now discharged, and it is worth saying which scene did it.

Lesson 01 asked what happens when a cell in the crypt stops obeying the arrangement, and said colorectal cancer is the clinical form of the failure. Scenes 5, 6 and this one. Lesson 02 said this lesson would return to the crypt when division stops being controlled. Scene 5. Lesson 04 established that phosphatidylserine on the outer surface of a dying cell is read as an instruction to engulf it, and handed forward how that removal is controlled. Scenes 2 and 3. Lesson 06 identified the joint that fails when a cell's position reading is decoupled, and left what happens next to this lesson. Scene 5. Lesson 07 said this lesson would return to where cells are shed and to what happens when the climb stops ending. Scenes 3 and 5.

Three questions leave this lesson unresolved, and they are unresolved in the literature rather than merely omitted here.

Whether shedding at an intestinal surface is caused by detachment or preceded by death is not known, and the review that examines it most closely says so and reports evidence on both sides. Which of p53's three responses does the tumour-suppressing work is not settled, and depends on the tissue. And the clearest evidence that normal tissue carries driver mutations while working normally comes from skin; this lesson has no colonic dataset of that kind, so its extension of that finding to the colon is a use of the model and not a measurement.

A lesson that closed those three would be a more satisfying lesson and a less accurate one.

A 2015 Science paper supplies the driver mutations in normal, functioning eyelid epidermis. A 2014 review of p53 supplies the unresolved question of which response carries its tumour suppression and the tissue-dependence of that answer. The section described in the worked example is constructed for this lesson. It is not a real specimen, not a real report, and describes no person. The colon-polyp density and extrusion observations it borrows are reported in the 2012 paper as a comparison between polyp and control sections, which is an association in tissue examined once, and that paper's own suggestion that retained cells may set the stage for tumour formation is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated causal chain. The six-step reading route, the judgement that step 3 is the step most often skipped, and the argument connecting per-cell replacement to per-cell removal and thence to the cost of continuous division, are this lesson's own. The gap-sealing interval is a small-intestinal measurement and is used here for the mechanism it describes rather than as a colonic figure. No dose, threshold, staging category, diagnostic criterion, screening interval or recommendation is taken from any source or stated anywhere in this scene.
